learning_objective: 🎯 Learn the traffic signals of reading and writing to give your sentences the perfect pauses, stops, and emotions!

main_concepts.concept_title: 🚦 Why Punctuate? (The Traffic Lights of English)
main_concepts.simple_explanation: Without punctuation, words crash into each other and make no sense! 'Let's eat grandma' sounds terrifying. 'Let's eat, grandma' is a nice invitation for dinner. Punctuation marks are the pauses, stops, and emotions of your writing.

main_concepts.concept_title: 🛑 The Big Three Ends (Full Stop, Question, Exclamation)
main_concepts.simple_explanation: A Full Stop (.) is a red light; the sentence is over. A Question Mark (?) is used when you ask something and expect an answer. An Exclamation Mark (!) shows strong emotion like shouting, surprise, or anger! Example: 'Watch out!'

A comma (,) is a yellow light—slow down and pause. Use it to separate items in a list (I bought apples, bananas, and milk). Use it after introductory words (Yes, I will go). Use it to separate two clauses connected by FANBOYS (I was tired, so I slept).

The apostrophe (') has two main jobs. 1) Ownership: to show something belongs to someone (Rahul's bag, the dog's bone). 2) Contraction: to squeeze two words into one by removing letters (Do not = Don't, I am = I'm).
When do you use Big Letters? Remember MINTS! M - Months and Days. I - The pronoun 'I'. N - Names of people, places, and brands. T - Titles of books and movies. S - Start of every new sentence!

fun_activity.title: 🕵️‍♂️ The Punctuation Fixer
fun_activity.instructions: Here is a messy sentence with zero punctuation or capitals: 'wow said rahul i cant believe we are going to delhi on monday'. Fix it using capitals, commas, apostrophes, and quotation marks!

quick_recap: ⭐ Punctuation gives sentences clear meaning and stops confusion.
⭐ Every sentence ends with a full stop, question mark, or exclamation mark.
⭐ Use commas to separate items in lists or to take a pause.
⭐ Apostrophes show ownership (Ravi's pen) or contractions (Can't).
⭐ Use the MINTS rule to remember when to capitalise words.
